cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.q: Why are electromagnetic interactions the dominant processes for charged particles and photons passing through matter?
cards.a: Because the Coulomb interaction is both strong and long-ranged. As a result, inelastic collisions with atomic electrons are by far the most probable interactions for charged particles and photons.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.q: Why do neutrons interact with matter differently from charged particles?
cards.a: Neutrons carry no electric charge and therefore do not undergo Coulomb interactions. Their dominant interactions with matter are due to the strong nuclear force, although electromagnetic interactions (through their magnetic moment) and weak interactions are also possible.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.q: In the definition of a scattering cross section, must the incident particle remain the same type of particle after the reaction?
cards.a: No. Here, scattering means any reaction in which an outgoing particle is emitted into the solid angle $\Omega$. The incident particle need not retain its identity.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.q:
The differential cross section is defined by
$$\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega}(E,\Omega)=\frac{1}{F}\frac{dN_s}{d\Omega}.$$
What do the quantities in this equation represent, and what is the physical meaning of $d\sigma/d\Omega$?
cards.a: $F$ is the flux of incident particles, measured as the number of particles per unit area per unit time, and $dN_s/d\Omega$ is the average number of particles scattered per unit time into unit solid angle around $\Omega$. Thus, $d\sigma/d\Omega$ is the average fraction of incident particles scattered into $d\Omega$ per unit time per unit incident flux. It measures the probability of a reaction producing an outgoing particle in a specified angular direction.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.q: How is the differential cross section defined?
cards.a:
The differential cross section is defined as

$$\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega}=\frac{1}{F}\frac{dN_s}{d\Omega},$$

where $F$ is the incident particle flux and $dN_s/d\Omega$ is the average number of particles scattered into the solid angle $d\Omega$ per unit time.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.q: What assumptions are made when defining the differential cross section?
cards.a: The incident beam is assumed to be much broader than the target, uniformly distributed in space and time, and characterized by a constant particle flux.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.q: What does the differential cross section represent physically?
cards.a: It represents the fraction of the incident flux that is scattered into a given solid angle per unit time.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.q: Why does the cross section have the dimensions of an area?
cards.a: Since the incident flux has units of particles per unit area per unit time, the definition of the cross section gives it the dimensions of an area. This motivates the heuristic picture of an effective target area, although it should not be interpreted as the physical size of the target.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.q: Why should the cross section not be interpreted as the physical size of the target?
cards.a: Although the cross section has units of area, it is an effective measure of interaction probability rather than the geometric size of the scattering center.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.q: On which quantities can the differential cross section depend?
cards.a: In general, the differential cross section depends on both the incident particle energy and the scattering angle.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.q: How is the total cross section obtained from the differential cross section?
cards.a:
The total cross section is obtained by integrating the differential cross section over all solid angles:

$$\sigma(E)=\int\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega}\,d\Omega.$$

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.q:
For a thin slab containing uniformly distributed interaction centers,
$$N_s(\Omega)=FAN\,\delta x\,\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega}.$$
Explain the physical origin of each factor.
cards.a: $FA$ is the number of incident particles per unit time that strike the target area $A$. The product $N\delta x$ is the number of interaction centers per unit area along the beam direction, where $N$ is their number density and $\delta x$ is the slab thickness. The differential cross section $d\sigma/d\Omega$ determines the probability for one incident particle to be scattered toward the specified solid angle.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.q:
The total number of particles scattered per unit time from a thin slab is
$$N_{\mathrm{tot}}=FAN\,\delta x\,\sigma.$$
Under what approximation is this expression valid?
cards.a: The slab must be sufficiently thin that the probability of one interaction center lying behind another, as viewed by the beam, is small. In this limit, attenuation and multiple interactions can be neglected, and the contributions from the interaction centers add independently.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.q:
For a particle crossing a thin thickness $\delta x$, the interaction probability is
$$\operatorname{Prob.\ of\ interaction\ in\ }\delta x=N\sigma\,\delta x.$$
What does this equation imply about the roles of $N$, $\sigma$, and $\delta x$?
cards.a: The interaction probability increases linearly with the density of available interaction centers $N$, the cross section $\sigma$ of each center, and the distance $\delta x$ traveled through the material. The relation applies in the thin-target limit, where this probability is small.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.q:
The probability that a particle suffers an interaction somewhere within a distance $x$ is
$$P_{\mathrm{int}}(x)=1-\exp(-wx),$$ where $w = N\sigma$. 
Why is this the complement of the survival probability?
cards.a: After traveling the distance $x$, the particle must either have survived without interaction or have interacted at least once. These mutually exclusive possibilities exhaust all outcomes, so the interaction probability is one minus the survival probability.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.q: What is the survival probability?
cards.a: The survival probability is the probability that a particle travels a distance $x$ through a material without undergoing an interaction.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.q:
The survival probability is
$$P(x)=e^{-wx}.$$
Why does the condition $P(0)=1$ fix the multiplicative constant in the general solution?
cards.a: At zero distance, the particle has not yet had an opportunity to interact, so its probability of survival must be unity. Applying this condition to $P(x)=C\exp(-wx)$ gives $C=1$.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.q:
The survival probability can be written as
$$P(x)=\exp\left(-\frac{x}{\lambda}\right)=\exp(-N\sigma x).$$
What is the significance of the ratio $x/\lambda$?
cards.a: The ratio $x/\lambda$ is the distance traveled expressed in units of the mean free path. The survival probability decreases exponentially as this dimensionless thickness increases.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.q:
The probability that a particle survives to $x$ and then suffers a collision between $x$ and $x+dx$ is
$$F(x)dx=w e^{-wx}\,dx.$$
Explain the two factors in this expression.
cards.a: The factor $\exp(-wx)$ is the probability that the particle reaches $x$ without interacting. The factor $w\,dx$ is the probability that it then interacts within the following infinitesimal interval $dx$. Their product gives the probability that the first collision occurs in that interval.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.q:
The mean free path is defined by
$$\lambda=\frac{\int xP(x)\,dx}{\int P(x)\,dx}=\frac{1}{w}.$$
What is the physical meaning of $\lambda$?
cards.a: $\lambda$ is the mean distance traveled by a particle before suffering a collision. Since $\lambda=1/w$, a large interaction probability per unit distance corresponds to a short mean free path, while a small interaction probability per unit distance corresponds to a long mean free path.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.q: How does the survival probability vary with distance?
cards.a:
The survival probability decreases exponentially with distance:

$$P(x)=e^{-wx}=e^{-N\sigma x},$$

where $N$ is the number density of interaction centers, $\sigma$ is the total cross section and $w dx$ is the probability of having an interaction between $x$ and $x + dx$.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.q: How is the mean free path related to the number density and the cross section?
cards.a:
The mean free path is

$$\lambda=\frac{1}{N\sigma}.$$

It decreases when either the number density of scattering centers or the interaction cross section increases.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.q: Why does a larger cross section lead to a shorter mean free path?
cards.a: A larger cross section means that the particle has a higher probability of interacting with each scattering center. Consequently, it travels a shorter average distance before suffering a collision.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.q: Why does a higher number density of scattering centers reduce the mean free path?
cards.a: Increasing the number density places more scattering centers along the particle's path, increasing the interaction probability and reducing the average distance between collisions.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.q: For a very thin target ($x\ll\lambda$), how can the interaction probability be approximated?
cards.a:
For a thin target,

$$P_{\rm int}(x)\approx N\sigma x=\frac{x}{\lambda},$$

obtained by keeping only the first-order term in the exponential expansion.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.q:
For a small thickness $\delta x$,
$$P_{\mathrm{int}}=1-\left(1-\frac{\delta x}{\lambda}+\cdots\right)\simeq\frac{\delta x}{\lambda}.$$
What approximation has been made, and what is its physical meaning?
cards.a: The exponential has been expanded in powers of $\delta x/\lambda$, and only the first-order term has been retained. This requires $\delta x\ll\lambda$, so the interaction probability across the layer is small and increases approximately linearly with thickness.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.q: Summarize the relationships between survival probability, interaction probability, and mean free path.
cards.a:
Survival probability:
$$P(x)=e^{-x/\lambda}.$$

Interaction probability:
$$P_{\rm int}(x)=1-e^{-x/\lambda}.$$

Mean free path:
$$\lambda=\frac{1}{N\sigma}.$$

A larger cross section or a higher density of scattering centers leads to a shorter mean free path and therefore a higher interaction probability.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.sub: Energy Loss of Heavy Charged Particles
cards.q: What are the two principal effects observed when a heavy charged particle passes through matter, and which atomic processes mainly produce them?
cards.a: The particle loses energy and is deflected from its incident direction. The energy loss is produced mainly by inelastic collisions with atomic electrons, while the deflection is produced mainly by elastic scattering from nuclei. Both processes occur many times per unit path length, so their cumulative effects determine the particle's motion through the material.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.sub: Energy Loss of Heavy Charged Particles
cards.q: Which two processes are primarily responsible for the passage of charged particles through matter?
cards.a:
1. Inelastic collisions with atomic electrons.

2. Elastic scattering from atomic nuclei.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.sub: Energy Loss of Heavy Charged Particles
cards.q: Which processes other than atomic collisions can occur when charged particles pass through matter?
cards.a: Other possible processes include Cherenkov radiation, nuclear reactions, and bremsstrahlung. For heavy charged particles, these occur much less frequently than atomic collisions.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.sub: Energy Loss of Heavy Charged Particles
cards.q: Which particles are considered heavy charged particles?
cards.a: Heavy charged particles include muons, pions, protons, alpha particles, and light nuclei. Heavy ions are usually treated separately because additional effects become important.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.sub: Energy Loss of Heavy Charged Particles
cards.q: Why are charged particles divided into electrons/positrons and heavy charged particles?
cards.a: The much larger mass of a heavy particle allows it to be treated as moving approximately along an undeviated trajectory during an individual collision with an atomic electron. This approximation is not valid for incident electrons or positrons, whose mass is equal to that of the target electrons.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.sub: Energy Loss of Heavy Charged Particles
cards.q: Which process is primarily responsible for the energy loss of heavy charged particles in matter?
cards.a: The energy loss of heavy charged particles is dominated by inelastic collisions with atomic electrons, which ionize or excite the atoms of the material.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.sub: Energy Loss of Heavy Charged Particles
cards.q: Why can heavy charged particles lose a substantial amount of energy even though each collision transfers only a small amount of energy?
cards.a: Each collision transfers only a small fraction of the particle's kinetic energy, but the enormous number of collisions occurring per unit path length produces a significant cumulative energy loss.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.sub: Energy Loss of Heavy Charged Particles
cards.q: What is the difference between soft and hard atomic collisions?
cards.a: In a soft collision, the transferred energy causes only excitation of the atom. In a hard collision, the transferred energy is sufficient to ionize the atom. In some hard collisions, the emitted electron has enough energy to produce substantial secondary ionization.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.sub: Energy Loss of Heavy Charged Particles
cards.q: What are $\delta$-rays or knock-on electrons?
cards.a: Knock-on ($\delta$) electrons are energetic recoil electrons produced during hard ionizing collisions. They can themselves produce significant secondary ionization.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.sub: Energy Loss of Heavy Charged Particles
cards.q: Why does elastic scattering from nuclei contribute little to the energy loss of heavy charged particles?
cards.a: The nuclei of most materials are much heavier than the incident particle, so only a small amount of kinetic energy is transferred in an elastic collision. Nuclear scattering therefore contributes mainly to changes in direction, while atomic-electron collisions dominate the energy loss.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.sub: Energy Loss of Heavy Charged Particles
cards.q: In what situation can elastic scattering from nuclei contribute significantly to the energy loss?
cards.a: When the target nucleus has a mass comparable to that of the incident particle, such as an alpha particle scattering from hydrogen.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.sub: Energy Loss of Heavy Charged Particles
cards.q: Why is it meaningful to describe the energy loss of heavy charged particles using an average stopping power?
cards.a: Although individual collisions are statistical, the large number of collisions occurring over a macroscopic path length makes the fluctuations small. The average energy loss per unit length therefore provides a useful description.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.sub: Energy Loss of Heavy Charged Particles
cards.q: What is the stopping power?
cards.a: The stopping power is the average energy loss of a charged particle per unit path length in a material, usually written as $$\frac{dE}{dx}.$$

cards.topic: Ch.2 Summary
cards.sub: Energy Loss of Heavy Charged Particles
cards.q: Summarize the mechanisms by which heavy charged particles lose energy in matter.
cards.a: Heavy charged particles lose energy primarily through inelastic collisions with atomic electrons, producing excitation and ionization. Hard collisions may generate energetic knock-on (δ) electrons. Elastic scattering from nuclei mainly changes the particle's direction and usually contributes little to the energy loss because nuclei are much heavier than the incident particle. The large number of atomic collisions allows the energy loss to be described by the average stopping power $$dE/dx.$$

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.q:
The mean energy loss of a heavy charged particle is described by
$$-\frac{dE}{dx}=2\pi N_a r_e^2m_ec^2\rho\frac{Z}{A}\frac{z^2}{\beta^2}\left[\ln\left(\frac{2m_e\gamma^2v^2W_{\max}}{I^2}\right)-2\beta^2-\delta-2\frac{C}{Z}\right].$$
What physical process does this formula describe, and what are the main particle and material dependences?
cards.a: The Bethe-Bloch formula gives the mean energy loss per unit path length caused mainly by inelastic collisions of a heavy charged particle with atomic electrons. The factor $\rho Z/A$ reflects the electron density of the absorber, $z^2$ gives the dependence on the incident-particle charge, and $1/\beta^2$ produces the large stopping power of slower particles. The logarithmic term contains the collision kinematics and atomic excitation scale, while $\delta$ and $C$ correct the high- and low-energy behavior.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.q:
The maximum energy transferred in one collision is
$$W_{\max}=\frac{2m_ec^2\eta^2}{1+2s\sqrt{1+\eta^2}+s^2},$$
where $s=m_e/M$ and $\eta=\beta\gamma$. For $M\gg m_e$,
$$W_{\max}\simeq2m_ec^2\eta^2.$$
What collision produces $W_{\max}$, and what does the approximation show?
cards.a: $W_{\max}$ is produced by a head-on or knock-on collision with an atomic electron. For a projectile much heavier than the electron, the maximum recoil-electron energy grows approximately as $\beta^2\gamma^2$, so faster particles can produce increasingly energetic $\delta$-rays.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.q:
The mean excitation potential enters the Bethe-Bloch formula through
$$\ln\left(\frac{2m_e\gamma^2v^2W_{\max}}{I^2}\right).$$
What is the physical meaning of $I$, and why is it usually obtained semi-empirically?
cards.a: $I$ is an effective atomic excitation energy, approximately related to the mean orbital frequency by $I\sim h\bar\nu$. More precisely, it is a logarithmic average over atomic excitation frequencies weighted by oscillator strengths. Since these oscillator strengths are unknown for most materials, $I$ is commonly deduced from stopping-power measurements or semi-empirical formulas.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.q: The density effect enters the Bethe-Bloch formula through the term $-\delta$. What causes this correction, and why is it important at high energy?
cards.a: The electric field of the incident particle polarizes the absorber. This polarization shields distant electrons from the full field, reducing the energy transferred in distant collisions. The correction becomes important at high energy because the range of impact parameters that would otherwise contribute to the stopping power increases with the particle velocity.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.q:
The shell correction enters the Bethe-Bloch formula through
$$-2\frac{C}{Z}.$$
Why is this correction required at low velocity?
cards.a: At low velocity, the speed of the incident particle becomes comparable to or smaller than the orbital velocities of the bound electrons. The assumption that the target electrons are initially stationary is then no longer valid, so the uncorrected Bethe-Bloch formula overestimates the stopping power.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.q: The plot below compares the Bethe-Bloch stopping power with and without the shell and density corrections. Why are the curves different mainly at low and high energies but nearly coincide near the minimum?
cards.a: At low energy, the shell correction accounts for the motion and binding of the atomic electrons. At high energy, the density effect suppresses distant collisions through polarization shielding. Near the stopping-power minimum, both corrections are relatively small, so the corrected and uncorrected curves are close.

figure.caption: Influence of the shell and density corrections on the Bethe-Bloch stopping-power curve.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.q: Why are the shell and density corrections generally sufficient for applying the Bethe-Bloch formula to elementary particles?
cards.a: Other effects, including ultrarelativistic radiation corrections, finite-projectile-mass effects, higher-order QED terms, internal structure and spin corrections, are usually negligible at approximately the $1\%$ level. Electron capture can be important for heavy ions at very low velocities, but it is not normally relevant for elementary particles.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.q:
Cherenkov radiation is emitted when
$$v_{\rm particle}>\frac{c}{n},$$
or equivalently
$$\beta n>1.$$
What is the physical meaning of this threshold condition?
cards.a: The charged particle must move faster than the phase velocity of light in the material, $c/n$. It does not move faster than light in vacuum; rather, it outruns the electromagnetic disturbance that propagates through the medium.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.q:
The diagram below shows the coherent wavefront produced by a charged particle traveling through a dielectric medium. Using
$$\cos\theta_C=\frac{1}{\beta n(\omega)},$$
explain why the radiation is emitted on a cone and how its opening angle depends on the particle velocity.
cards.a: The electromagnetic disturbances emitted along the particle's path add coherently along a conical wavefront, analogous to a shock wave. As $\beta$ increases above threshold, $1/(\beta n)$ decreases and the Cherenkov angle $\theta_C$ increases. The angle may also depend on frequency because the refractive index $n(\omega)$ is dispersive.

figure.caption: Formation of the Cherenkov radiation cone by a particle moving faster than light in the medium.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.q:
For a radiator of finite thickness $L$, the angular distribution contains the factor
$$\left|\frac{\sin\xi(\theta)}{\xi(\theta)}\right|^2,$$
with
$$\xi(\theta)=\frac{\omega L}{2\beta c}\left(1-\beta n\cos\theta\right).$$
What does this factor imply about the angular distribution of Cherenkov radiation?
cards.a: It has the form of a Fraunhofer-diffraction pattern. For a large radiator, it produces a sharp peak around the Cherenkov angle defined by $1-\beta n\cos\theta=0$. For a shorter radiator, the peak broadens, so the radiation is spread over a wider range of angles.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.q:
The energy radiated per unit path length is
$$-\frac{dE}{dx}=z^2\frac{\alpha\hbar}{c}\int \omega\,d\omega\left(1-\frac{1}{\beta^2n^2(\omega)}\right),$$
where the integral includes only frequencies satisfying $\beta n(\omega)>1$. What does this expression show about the dependence of Cherenkov radiation on particle charge and velocity?
cards.a: The radiated energy increases as $z^2$ and generally increases with $\beta$ once the particle is above threshold. However, even at relativistic energies, the Cherenkov energy loss is normally small compared with the energy lost through atomic collisions.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.q:
The number of Cherenkov photons emitted per unit path length and wavelength interval is
$$\frac{d^2N}{dx\,d\lambda}=\frac{2\pi z^2\alpha}{\lambda^2}\left(1-\frac{1}{\beta^2n^2(\lambda)}\right).$$
What are the main physical consequences of the factors in this equation?
cards.a: The photon yield scales as $z^2$, vanishes below the threshold $\beta n\leq1$, and increases as the particle velocity rises above threshold. The factor $1/\lambda^2$ means that more photons are emitted at shorter wavelengths.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.q: Why can Cherenkov radiation be used for particle identification?
cards.a: Emission occurs only when the particle exceeds the velocity threshold $\beta>1/n$, and the emission angle satisfies $\cos\theta_C=1/(\beta n)$. A detector can therefore determine whether a particle is above a chosen velocity threshold or measure its velocity from the Cherenkov angle. Combined with momentum information, this can distinguish particles of different masses.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.q: Why are photomultipliers commonly used to detect Cherenkov radiation?
cards.a: The number of Cherenkov photons produced over the useful optical wavelength range is not very large. Photomultipliers efficiently convert these weak light signals into measurable electrical current pulses.

cards.topic: Ch.2: Passage of Radiation Through Matter
cards.q:
For a detector sensitive between approximately $350$ and $550\,\mathrm{nm}$, the photon yield is
$$\frac{dN}{dx}=475z^2\sin^2\theta_C\ \text{photons/cm}.$$
What does this result imply for the design of a Cherenkov detector?
cards.a: The available number of photons per unit path length is modest and depends strongly on the particle charge and Cherenkov angle. Efficient light collection and sensitive photodetectors are therefore important, and a longer radiator can increase the total detected signal.
